paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning methods assume that the environment follows the same rules over time: actions have stable effects, and rewards are assigned consistently. Real applications can violate this assumption, making a policy learned from earlier experience less effective later. This paper develops a way to test whether those rules have changed and locate the times when changes occurred.

The proposed procedure uses a model-based, doubly robust approach in offline reinforcement learning, working with previously collected data. Its stated setting requires a certain degree of homogeneity. The method is designed to tolerate model misspecification while controlling false alarms, known as type-I errors, and retaining strong ability to detect actual changes, particularly with high-dimensional data.

Comparative simulations and an interventional mobile health example illustrate the method’s advantages. The findings connect detecting environmental changes with improving long-term rewards: identifying when historical experience reflects different conditions can matter for sequential decisions. The evidence supports this approach in the studied nonstationary settings.
icml-2023-a-robust-test-for-the-stationa.tldr: A doubly robust test detects changes in offline reinforcement learning environments while controlling false alarms under the studied conditions.

paragraphs: Observing how a system’s components change over time does not directly reveal which components are connected. This paper addresses that structural inference problem: given agents’ observed states across a time period, determine whether directed connections exist between them. Direction matters because a connection from one agent to another is a different relationship from the reverse.

The proposed framework, ALaSI, uses deep active learning to learn representations of connections with a relatively small amount of prior knowledge. It also introduces two message-learning pipelines, described as inter-scope and out-of-scope, grounded in information theory. These components are intended to make structural inference more effective for large dynamical systems.

The authors evaluate the framework on large datasets containing both simulated systems and real-world networks. They report more accurate connection inference than previous methods in both supervised and unsupervised learning settings. The contribution combines efficient use of prior knowledge with message learning for larger systems, rather than treating every connection as an isolated prediction.
icml-2023-active-learning-based-structur.tldr: ALaSI combines active learning and information-theoretic message learning to infer directed connections in large dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make classifiers withstand deliberately chosen input perturbations. Earlier work had already shown that images generated by diffusion models could help. This paper asks whether improvements in the image generator translate into further robustness gains, and reports that they do in the evaluated settings.

The authors use a diffusion model with better image quality and greater sampling efficiency than DDPM, requiring approximately 20 sampling steps. Their approach uses generated data without adding external datasets. This connects progress in image generation to robust classification: the generator supplies training material whose usefulness is measured through the resulting classifier’s resistance to attacks.

Under an infinity-norm perturbation budget of 8/255, the reported robust accuracies are 70.69% on CIFAR-10 and 42.67% on CIFAR-100. Under a Euclidean-norm budget of 128/255, CIFAR-10 accuracy reaches 84.86%. The authors report state-of-the-art RobustBench results, including improvements over previous approaches using external data, and additional positive results on SVHN and TinyImageNet. These findings apply to the specified threat models and evaluations.
icml-2023-better-diffusion-models-furthe.tldr: Higher-quality diffusion-generated images improve adversarial training, producing reported robustness gains without external datasets.

paragraphs: Distributed training requires machines to exchange substantial amounts of information. For large foundation models, this communication burden favors data centers with fast connections and makes slower, decentralized infrastructure harder to use. CocktailSGD addresses this bottleneck by reducing the amount of information that must travel between machines during training.

The framework combines random sparsification, top-K sparsification, and quantization. These techniques reduce communication by selecting subsets of values and representing retained values with lower numerical precision. The paper’s central idea is that combining the three can compress communication much more strongly than applying any one alone. A theoretical convergence analysis supports the benefit of this hybrid approach.

In fine-tuning experiments with language models containing up to 20 billion parameters, the authors report compression of up to 117 times without harming convergence. On a 500Mbps network, training incurs only about a 1.2-fold slowdown relative to data center networks. These results suggest that communication compression can make slower networks practical for the evaluated fine-tuning workloads.
icml-2023-cocktailsgd-fine-tuning-founda.tldr: CocktailSGD combines three compression techniques to fine-tune large language models efficiently over slower networks.

paragraphs: Social recommendation draws on two kinds of behavior: the items people consume and the people they connect with. Hidden influences on these behaviors can become tangled together in a user representation. This paper proposes CurCoDis to separate those influences jointly across the consumption and social environments, with the motivation of making recommendations more explainable and controllable.

The method learns from user-item interactions and the user-user social graph together. It divides the social graph into equally sized subgraphs while minimizing the number of connections cut between them. A curriculum weighting strategy then uses subgraph complexity, measured through Descartes’ rule of signs, to guide how those subgraphs contribute during training.

CurCoDis also introduces a prototype-routing optimization mechanism to achieve joint disentanglement across the two environments. Experiments on several real-world recommendation datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The reported result supports learning the two sources of user behavior together while explicitly separating their hidden factors; explainability and controllability provide the motivation for that representation design.
icml-2023-curriculum-co-disentangled-rep.tldr: CurCoDis jointly separates hidden factors in consumption and social behavior to improve social recommendation.

paragraphs: Increasing a transformer’s size does not automatically make good use of a limited training dataset. This paper studies the data-scarce regime, where a very large model must learn from disproportionately little data. The authors find that existing scaling power laws underestimate the severity of this problem: performance can decline substantially when training data is insufficient.

Their proposed remedy is model reuse. Instead of beginning the larger model’s training without this prior foundation, they initialize it using smaller models. This warm start changes how the larger model makes use of the available data. The approach addresses the relationship between model capacity and data supply through initialization rather than assuming that enough additional data will become available.

Empirically, model reuse restores the observed power-law behavior under the studied data scarcity conditions. The authors also report consistent performance improvements when repeatedly applying reuse to expand model size. These findings suggest that how a model is initialized can materially affect scaling behavior when data, rather than model capacity, is the limiting resource.
icml-2023-data-efficient-neural-scaling-.tldr: Initializing large transformers from smaller models improves their empirical scaling behavior when training data is scarce.

paragraphs: Behavioral analysis can require finding patterns spread across time, space, and multiple types of observations. This paper studies that challenge using sequential visual and touch behaviors. Its motivation is that machine learning may identify complex behavioral patterns that traditional assessments do not readily recognize, potentially supporting quantitative behavioral analysis.

The proposed model combines Deep Temporal Sets with Evidential Reinforced Attentions. Deep Temporal Sets captures temporal relationships and converts the input into a set-based representation. The attention component represents uncertainty in its policy network and uses that evidence to guide exploration of relevant regions in the behavioral data. Together, the components address both how behavior unfolds and where the model should focus.

The evaluation uses child-computer interaction data to distinguish children with Autism Spectrum Disorder from typically developing children. The authors report better performance than the comparison methods. These findings support the model’s usefulness for the studied behavioral discrimination task and its potential for objective analysis; the stated contribution is a pattern-discovery approach, rather than an established clinical diagnostic procedure.
icml-2023-deep-temporal-sets-with-eviden.tldr: DTS-ERA combines temporal representations and uncertainty-aware attention to identify patterns in multimodal behavioral sequences.

paragraphs: A Lipschitz bound limits how strongly a network’s output can change when its input changes. This paper introduces a way to construct fully connected and convolutional networks with guaranteed bounds measured using Euclidean distance. The guarantee matches the tightest-known bounds obtained through the semidefinite-program certification approach described in the paper.

The main contribution is a smooth mapping from unrestricted parameters to network weights satisfying that certification bound. The mapping is complete: a network meets the specified SDP bound exactly when the parameterization can represent it. This completeness concerns the SDP-certified set. It allows standard gradient-based training without repeatedly projecting weights into the constraint set or adding computationally expensive barrier terms.

The construction can be viewed as a new sandwich layer or as a parameterization of ordinary feedforward networks with sharing between neighboring layers. Image-classification experiments show improvements over previous approaches in both empirical and certified robust accuracy. The practical significance is that enforcing the stated sensitivity guarantee becomes part of the network’s parameterization itself.
icml-2023-direct-parameterization-of-lip.tldr: A complete, smooth parameterization enables standard gradient training of networks that satisfy specified SDP-based Lipschitz bounds.

paragraphs: Training neural networks requires storing intermediate activations for the backward pass, which can consume substantial memory. Existing activation-compression approaches can complicate training by searching for suitable numerical bit widths along the way. DIVISION proposes a simpler compression strategy based on differences between the information carried by activation-map components.

The motivating observation is that backward propagation mainly uses the low-frequency component, while caching the high-frequency component accounts for most of the activation memory. DIVISION therefore stores the low-frequency component at high precision and compresses the high-frequency component using lower numerical precision. The design assigns storage precision according to the components’ observed importance during training.

Experiments report more than tenfold compression of activation maps, competitive training throughput, and no loss of model accuracy in the evaluated settings. The authors also report better overall performance than state-of-the-art compression methods. These results concern activation storage specifically, and show that preserving every activation component at the same precision can be unnecessary for the tested networks.
icml-2023-division-memory-efficient-trai.tldr: DIVISION reduces activation memory by preserving low-frequency information at high precision and compressing high-frequency information.

paragraphs: Structural inference seeks to recover connections within a system from its observed behavior. This can be difficult when observations contain only a small number of trajectories or cover short periods. The paper proposes combining reservoir computing with a variational autoencoder framework to make better use of such limited data.

The underlying autoencoder uses bi-level optimization and follows the information bottleneck principle to infer an adjacency matrix in its latent representation. That matrix represents the system’s connections. A reservoir computing network takes over part of the decoder’s role and encourages additional gradient-descent steps with the available data. The contribution therefore changes how the inference framework learns from limited trajectories.

Experiments cover biological networks, simulated brain-imaging data, and physical simulations. The authors report effective and efficient structural inference using substantially fewer trajectories or much shorter trajectories than previous work. These findings suggest that incorporating reservoir computing can improve the data requirements of this structural inference framework across the evaluated types of dynamical systems.
icml-2023-effective-and-efficient-struct.tldr: Adding reservoir computing to a variational structural-inference framework enables effective connection recovery from fewer or shorter trajectories.

paragraphs: Observational data may leave several causal explanations compatible with what was measured, especially when relevant variables are unobserved. A partial ancestral graph represents this uncertainty by leaving some causal relationships unresolved. Different compatible causal graphs can imply different effects, so this paper aims to estimate the set of possible effects rather than force a single answer.

The approach focuses on effects obtainable through covariate adjustment. A direct strategy would enumerate all causal graphs compatible with the partial graph and examine their adjustment possibilities. That becomes expensive because the number of compatible graphs can grow super-exponentially with the number of variables. The authors introduce a graphical characterization of possible adjustment sets that avoids this enumeration.

Using that characterization, their method returns the same set of possible effects as the enumeration approach with super-exponentially less complexity. Experiments support both its effectiveness and substantial efficiency improvement. The result makes it more practical to retain causal uncertainty when latent variables and unresolved relationships prevent choosing one fully specified causal graph.
icml-2023-estimating-possible-causal-eff.tldr: A graphical method finds possible adjustment-based causal effects from a partial ancestral graph without enumerating compatible causal graphs.

paragraphs: A graph network trained to predict node classes does not necessarily produce representations that work well for clustering. Classification and clustering reward different properties, so useful grouping information can be absent from features learned for label prediction. GC-Flow addresses this mismatch by changing the probabilistic model behind graph representation learning.

The method replaces graph convolutional network layers with normalizing flows while retaining graph convolution operations. Instead of directly modeling class probabilities given node features, it models feature likelihoods conditioned on classes together with class probabilities. Its representation space follows a Gaussian mixture structure, giving the learned features an explicit organization that supports separated groups.

Benchmark experiments demonstrate that GC-Flow retains classification predictive power while producing well-separated clusters. The authors also find further clustering gains from additional parameterization, including parameterizing the adjacency matrix used in graph convolutions. The contribution shows how a generative objective and structured representation space can align graph learning more closely with clustering while preserving useful prediction capabilities.
icml-2023-gc-flow-a-graph-based-flow-net.tldr: GC-Flow combines graph convolutions with normalizing flows and a Gaussian mixture representation to improve clustering while preserving predictive power.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems reuse stored trajectories to train their models. When those models are large sequence networks such as transformers, supplying that experience can become a bottleneck in memory, computation, and communication. GEAR is a distributed experience replay system designed to address all three bottlenecks with a GPU-centered architecture.

The system manages trajectory data using both host memory and GPU device memory on GPU servers. It distributes trajectory-selection work across GPU devices so that selection does not become a centralized computational obstacle. For data movement, specialized GPU kernels access host memory without an intermediate copy, while remote direct memory access over InfiniBand supports efficient communication between machines.

Cluster experiments report performance up to six times that of Reverb when training large reinforcement learning models. This is a systems result about the infrastructure delivering training experience. The contribution shows how coordinating memory placement, trajectory selection, and communication can improve the performance of experience replay as the models consuming that experience grow larger.
icml-2023-gear-a-gpu-centric-experience-.tldr: GEAR reorganizes trajectory storage, selection, and transfer around GPUs to accelerate experience replay for large reinforcement learning models.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images without providing a compact representation whose coordinates correspond to meaningful properties. InfoDiffusion aims to combine these two capabilities. It adds low-dimensional latent variables intended to capture high-level sources of variation in the data, making the generator’s internal representation more useful for interpretation and manipulation.

The training objective includes a mutual-information regularizer linking observed data and hidden variables. This encourages the latent representation to retain meaningful information about the observations. It also addresses the possibility that a powerful diffusion decoder could produce samples while ignoring the added latents, which would undermine their usefulness as a representation.

Experiments find disentangled, human-interpretable representations competitive with state-of-the-art generative and contrastive approaches while maintaining diffusion models’ sample quality. The method also enables changing attributes of generated images through the learned representation. The authors identify generative design as a potential application, where exploring meaningful latent variations could help produce useful samples; that application is presented as a possibility.
icml-2023-infodiffusion-representation-l.tldr: InfoDiffusion uses mutual-information regularization to learn interpretable latent variables while retaining high-quality diffusion generation.

paragraphs: An agent often has to act without observing the full state of its environment. Its current observation may be insufficient, making memory and information gathering important. Standard deep reinforcement learning approaches that condition decisions on the entire interaction history can be difficult to train. This paper instead builds policy learning around learned belief-state representations.

The method uses state information during training that may be unavailable when the policy is deployed. It separates learning the belief representation, through unsupervised learning, from optimizing the policy through reinforcement learning. It also learns a compact representation of state features relevant to reward. This separation gives policy learning a more focused input than an undifferentiated interaction history.

Experiments demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness in partially observable domains requiring information seeking and long-term memory. The contribution brings a belief-modeling strategy associated with tabular partially observable problems into more complex deep learning settings. Its practical setup depends on access to additional state information during training, while allowing deployment without that same information.
icml-2023-learning-belief-representation.tldr: Learning compact belief representations separately from policies helps reinforcement learning agents handle partial observability and long-term memory.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning trains a model of environmental dynamics and uses its predictions to support policy learning. The data used to train that model often comes from a replay buffer containing experience from many earlier policies. This paper observes that fitting all historical experience does not necessarily give the best predictions for the policy currently being used.

As the policy changes, it visits different combinations of states and actions. The authors theoretically analyze how this distribution shift affects dynamics learning and model-generated rollouts. Their method, Policy-adapted Dynamics Model Learning, dynamically changes the mixture of historical policy distributions used for model learning so that the model can keep adapting to the evolving policy.

Experiments in MuJoCo continuous-control environments combine the method with state-of-the-art model-based reinforcement learning approaches. The authors report significant improvements in sample efficiency and higher eventual performance. The findings support aligning dynamics-model training with the current policy’s experience distribution, since an accurate fit to accumulated historical data may not be the most useful fit for present decisions.
icml-2023-live-in-the-moment-learning-dy.tldr: PDML adjusts dynamics-model training toward an evolving policy’s state-action distribution, improving reported sample efficiency and final performance.

paragraphs: Transformers are used across language, vision, speech, and multimodal learning, but their implementations differ between applications. One important difference is where normalization occurs within the network. Magneto seeks a common architecture that performs well across these settings and supports stable training as model scale increases.

The proposed design introduces Sub-LayerNorm to support expressivity and pairs it with an initialization strategy theoretically derived from DeepNet. These components address complementary concerns: how the architecture represents complex functions and how its parameters are initialized for stable scaling. The goal is a broadly useful Transformer design that reduces the need for different architectural variants across modalities.

Experiments span BERT-style and GPT-style language modeling, machine translation, BEiT vision pretraining, speech recognition, and BEiT-3 multimodal pretraining. The authors report stronger performance and better training stability than the established Transformer variants used for these applications. This breadth supports Magneto’s proposed role as a shared architecture across the evaluated tasks, with initialization and normalization treated as central design choices.
icml-2023-magneto-a-foundation-transform.tldr: Magneto combines Sub-LayerNorm and a theoretically derived initialization strategy to improve Transformer performance and stability across multiple modalities.

paragraphs: An agent may be uncertain about which environment model accurately describes the world. Robust reinforcement learning handles this by optimizing performance against the worst case within a specified collection of possible models. This paper studies that objective for average reward, focusing on model-free learning rather than requiring an explicitly learned environment model.

The theoretical starting point is the robust average-reward Bellman equation, which expresses the relationship underlying optimal decisions in this setting. The authors characterize the structure of its solutions and use that characterization to establish convergence results. They then develop two algorithms: robust relative value iteration TD and robust relative value iteration Q-learning.

The paper proves convergence of both proposed algorithms to the optimal solution within the analyzed setting. It also gives examples using several common uncertainty-set definitions, including contamination, total variation, Chi-squared divergence, KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance. The contribution connects a structural understanding of the robust decision equation to model-free algorithms whose optimization target explicitly accounts for uncertainty.
icml-2023-model-free-robust-average-rewa.tldr: Two model-free algorithms are proved to converge for robust average-reward reinforcement learning over specified environment uncertainty sets.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel in an image, making manual training labels expensive to collect. Semi-supervised methods also use unlabeled images, often assigning predicted labels to their pixels during training. When those predictions are unreliable, the resulting pseudo-labels can lead to poor segmentation.

NP-SemiSeg adapts neural processes to this setting to quantify uncertainty. Neural processes had previously been explored for semi-supervised image classification as an efficient approach to uncertainty estimation. Moving from classifying an entire image to labeling individual pixels brings that idea into a task where understanding uncertain predictions is especially relevant to the use of unlabeled training data.

The authors evaluate NP-SemiSeg on PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes under different training settings and report results supporting its effectiveness. The contribution is an adaptation of uncertainty-aware modeling to semi-supervised segmentation. Medical imaging and self-driving applications motivate the importance of unreliable pixel predictions in the paper; the stated experimental evidence comes from the two named public benchmarks.
icml-2023-np-semiseg-when-neural-process.tldr: NP-SemiSeg adapts neural processes to quantify uncertainty in semi-supervised pixel labeling.

paragraphs: Goal-reaching reinforcement learning requires an agent to learn how well it can reach a target from its current situation. The paper starts from a structural property of the optimal value function: it has a geometry called a quasimetric structure. That observation suggests designing the learning method around the structure the desired solution already possesses.

Quasimetric Reinforcement Learning uses quasimetric models to represent optimal value functions and introduces a learning objective tailored specifically to them. The contribution therefore involves both the model and the objective used to fit it. The authors provide strong theoretical recovery guarantees and analyze the method in a discretized MountainCar environment to examine its properties and advantages over alternatives.

Experiments also cover offline and online goal-reaching benchmarks with both state-based and image-based observations. Across these evaluations, QRL shows improved sample efficiency and performance. The findings support using the geometry of goal-reaching value functions as a learning constraint, connecting a task-specific mathematical property to practical improvements in the evaluated reinforcement learning problems.
icml-2023-optimal-goal-reaching-reinforc.tldr: QRL builds goal-reaching value learning around quasimetric structure, with theoretical recovery guarantees and reported empirical improvements.

paragraphs: A neural-network weight has both a magnitude and a polarity: its sign determines whether its contribution is positive or negative. This paper investigates whether setting those signs advantageously before learning can reduce training demands. Its motivation comes from biological development, where synaptic magnitudes change during learning while polarities remain largely stable.

The authors study this idea through simulations and image-classification tasks. They show that networks can learn with less time and data when weight polarities are adequately chosen in advance. This makes the initial sign configuration a meaningful part of the learning setup, with consequences for both the amount of evidence needed and the computation required.

The benefit is explicitly conditional on how the signs are set. The paper also demonstrates situations where choosing polarities beforehand disadvantages the network. Its conclusion is therefore about the value of suitable polarity configurations, not a universal advantage from fixing signs. The findings highlight a design choice that can influence statistical and computational efficiency during learning.
icml-2023-polarity-is-all-you-need-to-le.tldr: Adequately chosen weight polarities can reduce learning time and data needs, although preset polarities can also be disadvantageous.

paragraphs: A hypergraph allows one connection to involve several nodes. This paper studies recovering hidden communities in a symmetric model where every hyperedge joins the same number of nodes and communities have equal sizes. Hyperedge probabilities depend on the community memberships of the participating nodes, providing the statistical signal used for recovery.

The authors develop an iterative projected tensor power method to address the discrete, nonconvex maximum-likelihood problem. Their guarantee requires an initialization that already achieves partial recovery and applies in the logarithmic-degree regime. Under those conditions, the method recovers the entire hidden community structure with high probability down to the information-theoretic limit.

With the same initialization condition, the stated time complexity is O(n log² n / log log n), making the algorithm computationally competitive for the analyzed problem. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings. The contribution combines statistical accuracy near the recoverability boundary with efficient computation, while retaining explicit assumptions about the random hypergraph model and the quality of the starting point.
icml-2023-projected-tensor-power-method-.tldr: A projected tensor iteration achieves exact hypergraph community recovery at the information-theoretic limit under stated model and initialization conditions.

paragraphs: Slot attention can organize an image into representations of individual objects without supervision. However, the deterministic module does not itself provide a way to generate new scenes. Slot-VAE combines that object-centered representation ability with a hierarchical variational autoencoder, turning structured scene understanding into a basis for scene generation.

For each image, the model infers two connected levels of representation. A global representation captures the scene’s high-level organization, while individual slots encode object components. During generation, the model produces the object slots from the global representation. This dependency is intended to keep the generated components consistent with an overall scene structure.

The evaluation reports better sample quality and scene-structure accuracy than generative baselines built around slot representations. The contribution is the coordination between scene-level and object-level generation: objects are modeled as components of a coherent scene, with their representations conditioned on its global structure. The reported results support this hierarchical design for the evaluated scene-generation tasks.
icml-2023-slot-vae-object-centric-scene-.tldr: Slot-VAE generates structured scenes by conditioning object-level slots on a shared global scene representation.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds help relate a learning algorithm’s behavior on training data to its behavior on unseen data. This paper develops information-theoretic bounds within the supersample setting used by the conditional mutual information framework. Its aim is to obtain sharper guarantees from the relationship between training and testing losses in that setting.

The technical strategy projects a pair of losses, one from a training example and one from a testing example, into a single number. It then studies correlations between loss values and a random sign sequence, including shifted versions of that sequence. This provides a common route to several kinds of generalization bounds rather than only one particular inequality.

The resulting collection includes square-root bounds, fast-rate bounds involving variance and sharpness, and bounds for interpolating algorithms. The authors show through theoretical or empirical comparisons that these improve on previously known information-theoretic bounds in the same supersample setting. The significance is a tighter analysis within that framework, with different bounds addressing different aspects of learning behavior.
icml-2023-tighter-information-theoretic-.tldr: New loss-based information-theoretic analyses yield tighter generalization bounds within the supersample framework.

paragraphs: Starting online reinforcement learning from an offline-trained policy can speed improvement, but sometimes learning stalls. This paper investigates when a warm start helps actor-critic learning, particularly when function approximation makes the updates imperfect. The central question is how errors in the actor and critic affect the benefit of the initial policy.

The authors first quantify approximation errors in the two updates separately. They then interpret warm-start actor-critic as a perturbed version of Newton’s method, providing a mathematical framework for tracing how inaccurate updates affect performance over a finite learning period. Under general technical conditions, they derive upper bounds that clarify requirements for achieving desired learning performance.

The analysis identifies reducing algorithmic bias during online learning as essential in the studied framework. Lower bounds on the remaining suboptimality gap also quantify the effects of bias and error propagation. Together, these results explain why a promising initial policy alone may not ensure continued rapid improvement: the quality and accumulated effects of subsequent updates also matter.
icml-2023-warm-start-actor-critic-from-a.tldr: A perturbed-Newton analysis explains how actor-critic approximation errors and bias can limit the benefits of an offline warm start.
